Why LLM reinforcement learning breaks on robots, and how the frontier is fixing it

PPO and GRPO need the exact probability of each action, and actor-critics need a short path from the critic to the weights. A flow-matching robot policy offers neither, even in a simulator. This essay builds the flow policy, derives both RL families from one equation, shows where each one breaks, and walks through the fixes: RECAP, GVC, DSRL and QF3.

October 27, 202628 min readUpdated November 2, 2026

reinforcement-learningrobot-learningflow-matchingfoundation-models

Whole board

A friend who works on robots told me, almost in passing, that classic reinforcement learning is hard to do with flow matching. I nodded, then realized I couldn't say why. The language-model recipe looks simple: give the model a prompt, sample 64 answers, score them, and make the good ones more likely. That's GRPO, the update behind DeepSeek-R1, and a modern robot policy, a pretrained vision-language transformer with a small action head (a VLA), looks a lot like the model it trains. So why can't we copy the recipe?

There are two walls. The first is the environment. PPO needs fresh rollouts for every update, and GRPO needs its group of attempts to start from the same state, trivial for a text prompt and impossible for a crumpled shirt. A simulator knocks this wall down: Rudin et al. trained walking policies with 4,096 robots in parallel in Isaac Gym, and a simulator copies a start state as often as you like. A real robot can't throw data away, so it ends up with replay, bootstrapping and a neural critic, the deadly triad from part 5 of the RL series.

The second wall is the architecture, and it stands even in a simulator. A manipulation VLA like π0\pi_0π0​ refines noise into a whole second of motion over 10 steps with flow matching, and that design breaks both families of RL updates. This essay is about that wall: we'll build the flow policy, derive the two RL families from one equation, watch each one break, and end with the methods that get around it. The board on the side follows along.

1. A robot needs two good answers, and flow matching gives them

Averaging two good answers drives into the mug

Here's the running example. The robot reaches past a coffee mug. Half of the demonstrations go left, a=−1a = -1a=−1, and half go right, a=+1a = +1a=+1, and both work. Fit a network that outputs one number with squared error and it settles on the average, a=0a = 0a=0, straight through the mug. A mobile robot passing a pillar has the same two answers. Multimodality, several distinct good actions for one observation, is a hard constraint on the policy.

Language models get this for free from the softmax. Cut the action axis into bins, each with its own score ziz_izi​. The left demonstrations raise z−1z_{-1}z−1​, the right ones raise z+1z_{+1}z+1​, and since the probabilities ezi/∑jezje^{z_i} / \sum_j e^{z_j}ezi​/∑j​ezj​ share one denominator, bin 0 shrinks without a single demonstration of hitting the mug. The network also hands us the exact log⁡πθ(a∣s)\log \pi_\theta(a \mid s)logπθ​(a∣s) in one forward pass, which is what PPO and GRPO want.

Tokens keep both answers, but they come out one at a time

So why not tokenize robot actions? A robot action is many numbers that must agree. Take a robot with 29 joints controlled at 50 Hz: a one-second action chunk is 50×29=1,45050 \times 29 = 1{,}45050×29=1,450 numbers, and if the shoulder goes left of the mug, the elbow and wrist must go left too. Independent softmaxes sampled in parallel can send the shoulder left and the elbow right, so tokens have to come out one after another, each conditioned on the ones before, the way an LLM writes text.

Naive binning makes that 1,450 sequential tokens per chunk. Physical Intelligence's FAST (Pertsch et al., 2025) compresses each joint's trajectory with a discrete cosine transform (the JPEG trick: a smooth curve as a few cosine waves) and byte-pair encoding, to roughly 30 tokens per arm. Training is cheap, because the model predicts every known token in one parallel pass; the paper reports 5× fewer GPU hours than π0\pi_0π0​. Acting is slow, because each token waits for the last: on an RTX 4090, FAST π0\pi_0π0​ needs about 750 ms per chunk and flow-matching π0\pi_0π0​ under 100 ms. So π0.5\pi_{0.5}π0.5​ (arXiv:2504.16054) pretrains on FAST tokens and adds a flow-matching action expert, which is what runs on the robot.

Flow matching refines all 1,450 numbers at once

Flow matching takes the other road. Start from noise, a0∼N(0,I)a_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)a0​∼N(0,I), a 1,450-number chunk of static, and call a network K=10K = 10K=10 times, each call moving the whole chunk toward a clean motion. There are two clocks here, and I mixed them up at first. Robot time τ\tauτ runs over the 50 control steps inside the chunk. Denoising time ttt runs from 0 to 1 over the 10 network calls, and the robot doesn't move while it ticks. Drag the slider: each step changes all 1,450 numbers, and only at t=1t = 1t=1 does the robot play its second of motion.

The network is a velocity field vθ(at,t,s)v_\theta(a_t, t, s)vθ​(at​,t,s): given a half-finished chunk ata_tat​, the time ttt and the observation sss, it says which way to move. Training is plain regression. Take a recorded chunk a1a_1a1​ and noise a0a_0a0​, put a point on the straight line between them at a random ttt, and ask for the direction of that line:

at=(1−t) a0+t a1,LCFM(θ)=Et,a0,a1[∥vθ(at,t,s)−(a1−a0)∥2]a_t = (1 - t)\, a_0 + t\, a_1, \qquad \mathcal{L}_{\text{CFM}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{t, a_0, a_1}\Big[\big\| v_\theta(a_t, t, s) - (a_1 - a_0) \big\|^2\Big] at​=(1−t)a0​+ta1​,LCFM​(θ)=Et,a0​,a1​​[​vθ​(at​,t,s)−(a1​−a0​)​2]

This is conditional flow matching (CFM). In code, training and acting are a few lines each:

# train: one step on a batch of B recorded chunks
a1 = buffer.sample_chunks()   # (B, 50, 29)
a0 = randn_like(a1)           # noise
t  = rand(B, 1, 1)            # per-sample time in [0, 1]
at = (1 - t) * a0 + t * a1    # a point on the line
loss = ((v(at, t, s) - (a1 - a0)) ** 2).mean()

# act: 10 Euler steps from noise to a chunk
a = randn(50, 29)
for k in range(10):
    a = a + 0.1 * v(a, k / 10, s)

I had to stop at the target. At t=0.9t = 0.9t=0.9 we're nearly there, yet we still ask for the whole displacement a1−a0a_1 - a_0a1​−a0​. It doesn't overshoot because vvv is a speed, not a step: the sampler multiplies it by 0.1, so on a line from 0 to 1 the point at t=0.9t = 0.9t=0.9 moves to 0.9+0.1×1=1.00.9 + 0.1 \times 1 = 1.00.9+0.1×1=1.0 and lands exactly.

The clock input lets the streams split around the mug

If every training line has a constant speed, why does the network need ttt? Noise and demonstrations are paired at random, so some lines cross (top drawing). The line from +1+1+1 to −1-1−1 passes a=+0.5a = +0.5a=+0.5 at t=0.25t = 0.25t=0.25 with speed −2-2−2, and the line from −1-1−1 to +1+1+1 passes the same point at t=0.75t = 0.75t=0.75 with speed +2+2+2. Without the clock, the network sees one position with two opposite targets and learns their average, 0, back into the mug. With ttt it tells the two moments apart, and the learned field, the average of all lines through each point at each time, bends into the streams of the lower drawing. That's also why we take 10 small steps: one jump from t=0t = 0t=0 follows the averaged velocity into the middle.

Watch the shaded band. It starts wide and ends as a sliver at +1+1+1, the same probability packed into far less space. That squeeze is how a flow makes two modes out of one bell curve, and it's what will break family 1.

2. Two RL families come from one equation

Q-learning can't search 29 continuous joints

The oldest RL idea needs no policy network. With four Atari buttons, Q-learning scores each with a critic Qϕ(s,a)Q_\phi(s, a)Qϕ​(s,a), a network that predicts the return (total future reward), and presses the best. With 29 continuous joints there's nothing to enumerate: 10 bins per joint already makes 102910^{29}1029 combinations, and an argmax over space the critic never saw lands on whatever wild joint vector makes it spike. So we train an actor πθ\pi_\thetaπθ​ with weights θ\thetaθ, which means we need the gradient of the return.

The product rule splits on where θ lives

Write the expected return as a sum first, before any expectation:

J(θ)=∑aπθ(a∣s) Q(s,a)J(\theta) = \sum_a \pi_\theta(a \mid s)\, Q(s, a) J(θ)=a∑​πθ​(a∣s)Q(s,a)

Each term is how often we pick aaa times what it earns. During the actor update QQQ is a table of numbers: the true return, or a separate critic QϕQ_\phiQϕ​ trained with its own loss and held fixed while θ\thetaθ changes. With two actions, let θ\thetaθ be the probability of going right; left earns 2 and right earns 10, so J=(1−θ)⋅2+θ⋅10J = (1 - \theta) \cdot 2 + \theta \cdot 10J=(1−θ)⋅2+θ⋅10 and dJ/dθ=8dJ/d\theta = 8dJ/dθ=8. In general, the product rule gives

∇θJ=∑a[∇θπθ(a∣s)  Q(s,a)+πθ(a∣s)  ∇θQ(s,a)]\nabla_\theta J = \sum_a \Big[\nabla_\theta \pi_\theta(a \mid s)\; Q(s, a) + \pi_\theta(a \mid s)\; \nabla_\theta Q(s, a)\Big] ∇θ​J=a∑​[∇θ​πθ​(a∣s)Q(s,a)+πθ​(a∣s)∇θ​Q(s,a)]

and the two families differ only in which term survives. If the action aaa is a fixed point on the axis, θ\thetaθ lives in the probability alone and the second term is zero. If we write the action as a function of the weights, a=aθ(s,ϵ)a = a_\theta(s, \epsilon)a=aθ​(s,ϵ), then θ\thetaθ moves into QQQ's input and the second term is the one we use.

Family 1 divides by how often it sampled

A robot can't sum over every action; it tries a few and averages. Sampling from πθ\pi_\thetaπθ​ already weights each action by how often we pick it, so to recover the sum we divide each sample by its probability:

∇θJ=∑aπθ(a∣s) ∇θπθ(a∣s)πθ(a∣s) Q(s,a)=Ea∼πθ[∇θlog⁡πθ(a∣s)  A(s,a)]\nabla_\theta J = \sum_a \pi_\theta(a \mid s)\, \frac{\nabla_\theta \pi_\theta(a \mid s)}{\pi_\theta(a \mid s)}\, Q(s, a) = \mathbb{E}_{a \sim \pi_\theta}\big[\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a \mid s)\; A(s, a)\big] ∇θ​J=a∑​πθ​(a∣s)πθ​(a∣s)∇θ​πθ​(a∣s)​Q(s,a)=Ea∼πθ​​[∇θ​logπθ​(a∣s)A(s,a)]

The log comes from ∇π/π=∇log⁡π\nabla \pi / \pi = \nabla \log \pi∇π/π=∇logπ. I also swapped QQQ for the advantage A=Q−V(s)A = Q - V(s)A=Q−V(s), the return relative to the state's average, which leaves the expectation unchanged (probabilities sum to 1, so their gradients sum to 0) and changes the individual samples a lot. In the widget the policy goes right 10% of the time. Without the division the samples average to −0.8, the wrong sign. With it, 9 out of 10 samples still push θ\thetaθ toward the action that earns 2, until a rare right draw yanks it back with +100. Subtract V=2.8V = 2.8V=2.8 and every sample points the right way, still averaging 8.

This log-derivative trick is REINFORCE (1992), PPO (2017) and GRPO (2024). The advantage is an outside scalar on actions the robot actually executed: PPO gets it from a state critic Vϕ(s)V_\phi(s)Vϕ​(s), and GRPO from a group of real rollouts with no critic. Family 1 never asks how the return changes when you nudge the action, so a critic can't fool it with a spike at an untried action. In return it needs the exact log⁡πθ(a∣s)\log \pi_\theta(a \mid s)logπθ​(a∣s) and samples drawn from πθ\pi_\thetaπθ​ itself.

The second need is the environment wall in math. An action recorded by an older policy must be divided by the old probability instead, which gives PPO's ratio r(θ)=πθ(a∣s)/πold(a∣s)r(\theta) = \pi_\theta(a \mid s) / \pi_{\text{old}}(a \mid s)r(θ)=πθ​(a∣s)/πold​(a∣s) and its clipped objective

L(θ)=min⁡(rA, clip(r,0.8,1.2) A)L(\theta) = \min\big(r A,\ \text{clip}(r, 0.8, 1.2)\, A\big) L(θ)=min(rA, clip(r,0.8,1.2)A)

Past the clip the objective is flat, with zero gradient. Data from a policy that has since moved sits mostly on those plateaus and teaches nothing, hence the fresh rollouts.

Family 2 follows the critic's slope

The other branch puts θ\thetaθ inside the action. The simplest case is a deterministic actor a=μθ(s)a = \mu_\theta(s)a=μθ​(s), as in DDPG (2015) and TD3 (2018), and then there's no noise in the gradient at all, only the chain rule:

∇θJ=∂Qϕ(s,a)∂a∣a=μθ(s)⋅∇θμθ(s)\nabla_\theta J = \frac{\partial Q_\phi(s, a)}{\partial a}\Big|_{a = \mu_\theta(s)} \cdot \nabla_\theta \mu_\theta(s) ∇θ​J=∂a∂Qϕ​(s,a)​​a=μθ​(s)​⋅∇θ​μθ​(s)

A stochastic actor like SAC (2018) wants a distribution, and you can't backpropagate through a random number generator whose distribution depends on θ\thetaθ. The reparameterization trick moves the randomness outside: draw ϵ∼N(0,I)\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)ϵ∼N(0,I), which has no θ\thetaθ in it, and compute a=μθ(s)+σθ(s) ϵa = \mu_\theta(s) + \sigma_\theta(s)\, \epsilona=μθ​(s)+σθ​(s)ϵ, an ordinary function of the weights. A flow policy is already written this way. It draws a0a_0a0​ and runs 10 deterministic steps to get a1a_1a1​, so its ϵ\epsilonϵ is a0a_0a0​.

The payoff is signal. Family 1 learns from one number per sample, "this chunk was 5 better than average"; family 2 gets ∂Q/∂a\partial Q / \partial a∂Q/∂a, one slope for each of the 1,450 numbers, telling every joint which way to move. The cost is a learned action critic Qϕ(s,a)Q_\phi(s, a)Qϕ​(s,a) and a short differentiable path from θ\thetaθ to aaa. A learned critic can grow a spike where there's no data, which I'll call a critic mirage. The actor climbs onto it, and the Bellman backup r+γ Qϕ(s′,aθ(s′))r + \gamma\, Q_\phi\big(s', a_\theta(s')\big)r+γQϕ​(s′,aθ​(s′)) copies the inflated value to earlier states; TD3's twin critics and SAC's entropy bonus patch this loop.

On one sample, the two families can disagree

One more stop shows how differently the two families see the world. Give the robot one joint, a wrist torque aaa, a true return Q(a)=8−(a−1.5)2Q(a) = 8 - (a - 1.5)^2Q(a)=8−(a−1.5)2 that peaks at 1.5, and a Gaussian policy at μ=0\mu = 0μ=0 with σ=1\sigma = 1σ=1, whose average return is V=4.75V = 4.75V=4.75. Sample a=2.0a = 2.0a=2.0, just past the peak. It earns 7.75, an advantage of +3+3+3, so family 1 moves μ\muμ by A (a−μ)/σ2=+6A\,(a - \mu)/\sigma^2 = +6A(a−μ)/σ2=+6, toward the sample. Family 2 reads the slope under the sample, −1-1−1, times ∂a/∂μ=1\partial a / \partial \mu = 1∂a/∂μ=1, and moves μ\muμ back toward the peak. One sees height above average, the other the slope underfoot, and every sample in the shaded bands, between 1.5 and 3.3 or between −0.3 and 0, splits them.

Averaged over the whole bell, both give exactly +3+3+3, the true gradient, and the widget shows them agree for any μ\muμ. Here QQQ is the real return; a learned critic would lead family 2 onto its mirages.

3. A flow policy breaks both families

Family 1 needs a density, and the flow hides it in a squeeze

Now plug the flow policy into family 1. PPO wants log⁡πθ(a1∣s)\log \pi_\theta(a_1 \mid s)logπθ​(a1​∣s), the log-density of the chunk we executed. My first reaction: we can sample the policy as often as we like, so don't we know its distribution? But sampling gives you points, and a density is a statement about space. Remember the shaded band. A slice of noise of width 1.0 holding 30% of the probability ends up at width 0.01, so the density there is 0.3/0.01=300.3 / 0.01 = 300.3/0.01=30, a hundred times higher. Following one particle tells you where it landed, not how much its neighbors got squeezed. Counting samples fails too: halving each of the 1,450 axes already makes 214502^{1450}21450 boxes, so no other sample lands near yours, and a count has no gradient anyway.

The exact answer is the change-of-variables formula. The starting density p0p_0p0​ is a plain Gaussian with no θ\thetaθ in it, so all of θ\thetaθ's influence sits in how much the flow squeezed space along the path:

log⁡πθ(a1∣s)=log⁡p0(a0)−∫01tr⁡ ⁣(∂vθ(at,t,s)∂at)dt\log \pi_\theta(a_1 \mid s) = \log p_0(a_0) - \int_0^1 \operatorname{tr}\!\left(\frac{\partial v_\theta(a_t, t, s)}{\partial a_t}\right) dt logπθ​(a1​∣s)=logp0​(a0​)−∫01​tr(∂at​∂vθ​(at​,t,s)​)dt

The trace, the sum of the diagonal of a 1,450 × 1,450 Jacobian, is the expensive part. One backward pass gives you one row of that matrix, so you keep one diagonal entry and drop the other 1,449. Click through it: 1,450 backward passes for one Euler step, 14,500 for the chunk, where sampling took 10 forward passes. Then PPO wants the gradient of all that with respect to θ\thetaθ.

We can't design the squeeze away. Splitting one bell into two modes means stretching space in the middle and squeezing it at the modes, so a nonzero trace is the price of multimodality. And a simulator doesn't help, because this wall is made of compute, not data.

What if we constrain the Jacobian?

We can make likelihoods cheap by constraining the flow. SAC-NF (arXiv:1905.06893), NFPO (arXiv:2603.11470), PrT-Flow (arXiv:2610.17667) and GenPO++ (arXiv:2606.06967) use triangular Jacobians or reversible flows. Spectral normalization bounds the Jacobian instead, as Shin et al. (2025) do to make humanoid locomotion policies Lipschitz. Bi-Lipschitz constraints limit what each layer can express (Verine et al., 2021), and every one of these designs rules out the unconstrained transformer action expert that π0\pi_0π0​ uses.

Family 2 gets one backward pass, through nine multiplied Jacobians

Family 2 skips densities. The flow is already reparameterized, so PyTorch can backpropagate the critic's slope ∇a1Qϕ(s,a1)\nabla_{a_1} Q_\phi(s, a_1)∇a1​​Qϕ​(s,a1​) through the 10 Euler steps in a single backward pass. The trouble is what that pass multiplies. Each step feeds the next, at+0.1=at+0.1 vθ(at,t,s)a_{t + 0.1} = a_t + 0.1\, v_\theta(a_t, t, s)at+0.1​=at​+0.1vθ​(at​,t,s), so the first step's share of the gradient reaches the critic through nine Jacobians in a row:

g1=∂Qϕ∂a1 J10J9⋯J2 ∂a0.1∂θ,Jk=I+0.1 ∂vθ∂a∣step kg_1 = \frac{\partial Q_\phi}{\partial a_1}\, J_{10} J_9 \cdots J_2\, \frac{\partial a_{0.1}}{\partial \theta}, \qquad J_k = I + 0.1\, \frac{\partial v_\theta}{\partial a}\Big|_{\text{step } k} g1​=∂a1​∂Qϕ​​J10​J9​⋯J2​∂θ∂a0.1​​,Jk​=I+0.1∂a∂vθ​​​step k​

This is backpropagation through a 10-layer recurrent network. If each factor stretches some direction by 1.3, that direction grows by 1.39≈10.61.3^9 \approx 10.61.39≈10.6; at 0.7 it shrinks to 0.79≈0.040.7^9 \approx 0.040.79≈0.04. And the signal being warped is the critic's slope in 1,450 dimensions, where real coordinated motions occupy a thin sheet and the critic has seen nothing off it. The amplified slope pulls the chunk off the sheet, toward the mirages from section 2, now behind nine amplifiers.

Two PPO patches dodge the trace and pay elsewhere

DPPO (Ren et al., 2024), and πRL (Chen et al., 2025) for flow VLAs, keep PPO by treating each denoising step as its own action. Then we only need the probability of one small step, except the step is deterministic. If the old network moved a point from 0 to 0.200 and the updated one moves it to 0.201, the recorded 0.200 now has probability zero and log-probability −∞-\infty−∞. So they inject Gaussian noise into every step, making each one a small Gaussian policy with a one-line log-probability. The random start a0a_0a0​ already makes rollouts diverse, but diversity isn't a likelihood, so GRPO would need this noise as much as PPO. The cost is the horizon: 50 chunks become 50×10=50050 \times 10 = 50050×10=500 decisions, and the final reward must be spread over every noise kick inside the sampler.

FPO (McAllister et al., 2025) keeps the flow deterministic and estimates the ratio instead, using the change in flow-matching loss toward a1a_1a1​ as a stand-in for the change in log⁡πθ\log \pi_\thetalogπθ​. Here's my reading of where that gets loose. The loss is measured at sampled points (a0,t)(a_0, t)(a0​,t), one velocity at a time, while the real output comes out of 10 chained steps, where a small early tilt can send the chunk somewhere else. The true ratio can then leave [0.8,1.2][0.8, 1.2][0.8,1.2] while the estimate stays inside, and the clip stays open. In the π0.6∗\pi^*_{0.6}π0.6∗​ paper (arXiv:2511.14759), Physical Intelligence compared RECAP with a PPO variant built on DPPO and FPO, and with AWR, on real laundry folding: both baselines reached reasonable success rates and fell far short of RECAP's throughput.

4. Family 3 moves the reward into the input

Both families ask the flow for something it can't give cheaply. The next idea is to stop asking: keep training the flow with plain flow-matching regression, which it's great at, and bring the reward in another way.

AWR can only pull, so RECAP learns both and subtracts later

Advantage-weighted regression, AWR (Peng et al., 2019), multiplies each loss term by w=eA/βw = e^{A/\beta}w=eA/β. The weight must stay positive, because a negative weight on a squared error has no floor: the network could make that error as large as it likes. A bad sample can only get a weight near zero, and the π0.6∗\pi^*_{0.6}π0.6∗​ paper notes that such methods "discard or significantly downweight a significant portion of the data". Nothing pushes the policy away from a bad action.

RECAP (π0.6∗\pi^*_{0.6}π0.6∗​) gets the push elsewhere. A value network Vϕ(s)V_\phi(s)Vϕ​(s), predicting a distribution over 201 return bins, gives each chunk an advantage, and a percentile threshold turns it into one more text input, "Advantage: positive" or "Advantage: negative". Training is ordinary unweighted flow matching on all of the data, label included, with the label dropped 30% of the time so the same network also learns the unlabeled velocity. One network now knows what the data does on average and what its good part does, like an LLM that can follow either of two prompts.

The subtraction happens at test time, on velocities instead of in the loss. Query the network twice per Euler step, with and without the label, and extrapolate:

vguided=vall+β (vgood−vall)v_{\text{guided}} = v_{\text{all}} + \beta\, \big(v_{\text{good}} - v_{\text{all}}\big) vguided​=vall​+β(vgood​−vall​)

This is classifier-free guidance (CFG). On the board the good velocity is (0.7,1)(0.7, 1)(0.7,1) and the bad one (−0.3,1)(-0.3, 1)(−0.3,1). If 30% of the data near this point is good, vall=0.3 (0.7,1)+0.7 (−0.3,1)=(0,1)v_{\text{all}} = 0.3\,(0.7, 1) + 0.7\,(-0.3, 1) = (0, 1)vall​=0.3(0.7,1)+0.7(−0.3,1)=(0,1), and β=2\beta = 2β=2 gives (0,1)+2 (0.7,0)=(1.4,1)(0, 1) + 2\,(0.7, 0) = (1.4, 1)(0,1)+2(0.7,0)=(1.4,1), twice as far sideways as the good velocity and away from the bad one. (The mix changes across the flow with which kind of data probably produced the current point.)

# label once, with the 201-bin value network V
for chunk in buffer:
    chunk.I = "positive" if advantage(V, chunk) > threshold else "negative"

# train: plain flow-matching BC on 100% of the data, with the label as an input
# (dropping I on 30% of the steps teaches the unlabeled v_all)
loss = ((v(at, t, s, I) - (a1 - a0)) ** 2).mean()

# act: two network calls per Euler step
for k in range(10):
    v_all  = v(a, k / 10, s, I=None)
    v_good = v(a, k / 10, s, I="positive")
    a = a + 0.1 * (v_all + 2.0 * (v_good - v_all))

Try it on the mug, seen from above, where each point is where the gripper passes. Clean left and right passes are labeled positive; crashes and brushes are negative. At β=0\beta = 0β=0 with 10 steps, the samples reproduce all five clusters, crashes included. Raise β\betaβ and they move to the clean passes. Drop to one step and everything collapses to the average, inside the mug.

Labels go on chunks, not episodes. If a robot folds a sleeve perfectly and drops the shirt 20 seconds later, the episode's return calls the whole thing bad, while the value network sees the expected return jump after the good fold and labels that chunk positive.

Reward-conditioned cloning is older than Physical Intelligence

I first took this family for Physical Intelligence's invention. Reward-weighted regression goes back to Peters and Schaal (2007). Conditioning on the return instead of weighting by it came with Upside-Down RL (Schmidhuber, 2019; Srivastava et al., 2019) and the Decision Transformer (Chen et al., 2021), and Decision Diffuser (Ajay et al., 2022) added classifier-free guidance on returns to a diffusion model. RECAP conditions on a learned per-chunk advantage instead of an episode's return, and runs guidance on a billion-parameter flow VLA over rounds of real robot data.

GVC turns the generator into a critic

π0.7\pi_{0.7}π0.7​ (arXiv:2604.15483) widens the label to a quality score from 1 to 5, episode speed, per-segment mistake flags and generated subgoal images. The Generative Value Classifier, GVC (Swerdlow, Dong and Finn, 2026), points the same trick at the critic. A standard critic Qϕ(s,a)Q_\phi(s, a)Qϕ​(s,a) reads 1,450 action numbers and is graded on one output, the return. GVC makes the return, cut into KKK bins z1,…,zKz_1, \dots, z_Kz1​,…,zK​, an input, and predicts the action velocity, so the loss grades all 1,450 outputs:

∥vθ(at,t,s,zi)−(a1−a0)∥2\big\| v_\theta(a_t, t, s, z_i) - (a_1 - a_0) \big\|^2 ​vθ​(at​,t,s,zi​)−(a1​−a0​)​2

To score a candidate chunk aaa, GVC asks which return bin explains it best. A low flow-matching error under bin ziz_izi​ stands in for a high log⁡p(a∣s,zi)\log p(a \mid s, z_i)logp(a∣s,zi​), and Bayes' rule turns those into probabilities over bins:

p(zi∣s,a)=p(a∣s,zi) p(zi∣s)∑jp(a∣s,zj) p(zj∣s),QGVC(s,a)=∑ip(zi∣s,a) zip(z_i \mid s, a) = \frac{p(a \mid s, z_i)\, p(z_i \mid s)}{\sum_j p(a \mid s, z_j)\, p(z_j \mid s)}, \qquad Q_{\text{GVC}}(s, a) = \sum_i p(z_i \mid s, a)\, z_i p(zi​∣s,a)=∑j​p(a∣s,zj​)p(zj​∣s)p(a∣s,zi​)p(zi​∣s)​,QGVC​(s,a)=i∑​p(zi​∣s,a)zi​

A value anchor fits this QQQ to the bootstrapped temporal-difference target. At test time the policy samples NNN chunks (8 in most of the paper's benchmarks) and GVC executes the best one.

cands = [policy.sample(s) for _ in range(8)]

def q_gvc(a):
    err = array([flow_error(a, s, z) for z in bins])   # same (a0, t) for every bin
    p = softmax(-err + log_prior(s))                   # -err stands in for log p(a | s, z)
    return (p * bins).sum()                            # expected return

execute(max(cands, key=q_gvc))

But wait, this is the flow-error proxy I blamed for FPO's loose clip. Here it works for three reasons. Nothing takes a gradient step through it, so a bad score can't wreck the weights. All KKK bins are scored at the same (a0,t)(a_0, t)(a0​,t), so much of the sampling noise cancels in Bayes' rule. And GVC only ranks chunks the policy itself proposed, which all sit on the sheet of real motions, so the critic never gets to search empty space for a mirage.

5. Family 4 searches beyond the dataset

Family 3 has a ceiling. Guidance and best-of-NNN choose among behaviors the data already contains, and RECAP climbs one round of new robot data at a time. To find a motion nobody demonstrated, say pinning a box flap with one gripper while folding with the other, you need a critic's slope again, without the nine Jacobians.

DSRL steers the noise of a frozen flow

DSRL (Wagenmaker et al., 2025) never touches the flow's weights. A small RL policy chooses the starting noise a0a_0a0​, and the frozen flow turns it into a chunk; the paper applies this to π0\pi_0π0​. Every a0a_0a0​ decodes into a motion the flow knows how to make, so the search stays on the sheet and no gradient crosses the 10 steps. It finds the best of the flow's repertoire and stays inside it.

QF3 tilts the velocity with a one-step preview

QF3 (Kim et al., 2026) updates the flow with the critic's slope, through one step only. Recall the speed-times-time trick: at any point ata_tat​, holding the current velocity for the remaining time previews the endpoint,

a^1=at+(1−t) vθ(at,t,s)\hat{a}_1 = a_t + (1 - t)\, v_\theta(a_t, t, s) a^1​=at​+(1−t)vθ​(at​,t,s)

QF3 evaluates the critic's slope at a^1\hat{a}_1a^1​ and nudges vθv_\thetavθ​ toward a better endpoint, with the flow-matching loss kept on as an anchor. The velocity goes straight into the critic, never through nine more calls of vθv_\thetavθ​, so the product of Jacobians disappears. "Filtered" means the slope only reaches velocity coordinates that stay close to the replay data. The paper trains humanoid locomotion from scratch and transfers it to hardware, 10× faster in wall-clock time than FPO++.

The board lines up the four fixes against the two traps. Only QF3 sends the critic's slope back into the flow's weights, and it can because the slope crosses one step instead of ten.

My guess at the next step: imagine, score, distill

The published pieces suggest a loop I haven't seen in one paper, so read this part as my own synthesis. Max Bennett's book on the evolution of intelligence describes animals learning to simulate actions before taking them, and robots are getting the parts for that:

  • Rank with a world model at test time. GPC (Qi et al., 2025) forecasts a frozen diffusion policy's proposals and ranks them. FOREWARN (Wu et al., 2025) imagines plans in a latent world model and lets a VLM choose. VeriVLA (Sun et al., 2026) ranks flow-VLA chunks by predicted task progress.
  • Train on imagined rollouts. Ctrl-World (Guo et al., 2025) fine-tunes a policy on successful rollouts synthesized in its world model. World-Env (Xiao et al., 2025) runs RL post-training inside one.
  • Distill what was selected. Verify, Act, Distill (Hiratsuka et al., 2026) picks chunks with a learned verifier and distills successful episodes into the policy.

Put together, the flow policy proposes 16 chunks, a world model imagines each from the same starting state, GVC scores the outcomes, the robot executes the best, and the winner goes back into training with plain flow matching:

while True:
    s = observe()
    cands  = [flow_policy.sample(s) for _ in range(16)]     # propose
    future = [world_model.rollout(s, a) for a in cands]     # imagine, all from s
    best   = argmax([gvc_score(f) for f in future])          # score
    execute(cands[best])                                     # act
    buffer.add(s, cands[best])                               # distill on the next pass

The world model gives GRPO the one thing a real shirt never could, a group of attempts from the identical state, and regression on the winner replaces the ∇θlog⁡πθ\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta∇θ​logπθ​ a flow can't provide. It's GRPO in imagination, without the log-probability.

When the next robot RL paper comes out, two questions place it on this board: does it need the policy's log-probability, and does the critic's slope cross the sampler? A yes to either means it pays one of the bills from section 3, and the paper is really about how it pays.

Book: Max Bennett, A Brief History of Intelligence (2023). For the value-learning background, see Breaking Bellman and the RL series on this blog.
